content: The optimal intravenous fluid for kidney transplantation has not yet been definitively established, although normal saline is commonly used during the peri-operative period. Normal saline contains a high concentration of chloride, which has been linked to an increased risk of hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis. This condition may subsequently elevate the risk of hyperkalaemia and delayed graft function. In contrast, balanced electrolyte solutions have a lower chloride content, which may reduce these risks and potentially eliminate the need for dialysis due to hyperkalaemia in the immediate post-transplant period. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) investigating this issue have primarily focused on biochemical outcomes to compare these fluids. However, these studies have generally been underpowered to evaluate patient-centered outcomes, such as delayed graft function. The objective of this review was to assess the impact of lower-chloride solutions compared to normal saline on delayed graft function, hyperkalaemia, and acid-base balance in kidney transplant recipients. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant's Specialised Register was performed up to November 26, 2015. The search was facilitated by an Information Specialist and utilized terms relevant to the topic. The inclusion criteria were RCTs involving kidney transplant recipients that compared peri-operative intravenous lower-chloride solutions to normal saline. Two independent investigators evaluated the studies for eligibility and assessed the risk of bias. Data from individual studies were extracted using standardized forms and analyzed according to a pre-specified protocol. Summary estimates of effect were calculated using a random-effects model. Results were expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for dichotomous outcomes, and mean differences (MD) with 95% CI for continuous outcomes. The review included six studies with a total of 477 participants, all of whom were adult kidney transplant recipients. Approximately 70% of the participants underwent live-donor kidney transplantation. The overall risk of bias was low for selection bias but unclear for other domains. There was no significant difference in the risk of delayed graft function between participants who received balanced electrolyte solutions and those who received normal saline (3 studies, 298 participants: RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.70). Similarly, no significant difference was observed in the risk of hyperkalaemia (2 studies, 199 participants: RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.04 to 6.10). However, the use of intraoperative balanced electrolyte solutions, compared to normal saline, was associated with higher blood pH levels (3 studies, 193 participants: MD 0.07, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.09), higher serum bicarbonate levels (3 studies, 215 participants: MD 3.02 mEq/L, 95% CI 2.00 to 4.05), and lower serum chloride levels (3 studies, 215 participants: MD -9.93 mmol/L, 95% CI -19.96 to 0.11). In terms of clinical outcomes, there were four cases of graft loss in the normal saline group compared to one case in the balanced electrolyte solution group. Additionally, there were four cases of acute rejection in the normal saline group, whereas only two cases were reported in the balanced electrolyte solution group. In conclusion, balanced electrolyte solutions are associated with a reduced incidence of hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis compared to normal saline. However, it remains uncertain whether the use of lower-chloride solutions translates into improved graft outcomes when compared to normal saline.
